## Solution

**Claim:** Yes. There exists a countable collection $\{A_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ of subsets of $[0,1]$ such that $\{\bigcap_{i\in J} A_i : J\subseteq\mathbb{N},\ |J|=\infty\}$ is uncountably infinite.

### Construction

Choose any sequence of **distinct** points $\{x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots\} \subseteq [0,1]$ (possible since $[0,1]$ is uncountable). Define

$$A_i := [0,1] \setminus \{x_i\}, \qquad i \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Each $A_i$ is a subset of $[0,1]$, and the collection $\{A_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ is countable.

### The intersection indexed by an infinite $J$

For any infinite $J \subseteq \mathbb{N}$,

$$\bigcap_{i \in J} A_i \;=\; \bigcap_{i \in J}\bigl([0,1]\setminus\{x_i\}\bigr) \;=\; [0,1] \setminus \bigcup_{i\in J}\{x_i\} \;=\; [0,1]\setminus\{x_i : i\in J\}.$$

### Injectivity: distinct infinite $J$ give distinct intersections

Let $J, J' \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be two **distinct** infinite sets. Without loss of generality there exists $i_0 \in J \setminus J'$. Then:

- $x_{i_0} \in \{x_i : i \in J\}$, so $x_{i_0} \notin \bigcap_{i\in J} A_i$.
- Since $i_0 \notin J'$ and the points $\{x_i\}$ are all distinct, $x_{i_0} \notin \{x_i : i \in J'\}$, so $x_{i_0} \in \bigcap_{i\in J'} A_i$.

Therefore $\bigcap_{i\in J} A_i \neq \bigcap_{i\in J'} A_i$.

### Cardinality conclusion

The map

$$J \longmapsto \bigcap_{i\in J} A_i$$

is **injective** on the family of all infinite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. The set of infinite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$ (uncountable). Hence

$$\left|\left\{\bigcap_{i\in J} A_i : J\subseteq\mathbb{N},\ |J|=\infty\right\}\right| = 2^{\aleph_0},$$

which is uncountably infinite. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
